deal_summary: An equipment proposal led to customer and director review, contract preparation, and a stated payment date; repeated payment follow-up reportedly irritated the customer, while a separate filling-line need appeared late in the record (evidence 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).

customer_need.summary: A manager log describes a labeling project for cylindrical PET containers with a purchase target in August; later customer messages request a specification, commissioning work, and an invoice (evidence 0, 2).

deal_dynamics.early: The seller sent a quote and video; the customer sent packaging information and asked to move to a specified contract (evidence 1, 2).
deal_dynamics.middle: The decision depended on a director's review, followed by legal review and a signed-document exchange (evidence 3, 4).
deal_dynamics.late: The customer stated a Tuesday payment date; a manager worklog reports irritation with repeated payment checks, and a later call introduces another filling-line scope (evidence 5, 6, 7).

positive_signals: The customer requested contract preparation and gave a payment date (evidence 2, 5).
The customer later supplied technical information about a four-doser filling block for two canister types (evidence 7).
negative_signals: The customer could not obtain a decision from the director during the review period (evidence 3, 4).
A manager worklog says the customer reacted negatively to repeated payment reminders; this is not a direct customer quote (evidence 6).
customer_behavior.initiative: The customer supplied specifications, requested commissioning work, and asked how to handle payment coordination (evidence 2, 5, 7).
customer_behavior.decision_process: The labeling purchase went through director and contract review; a separate filling-line discussion also involved technical clarification. The view does not establish whether both scopes belonged to one purchase (evidence 3, 4, 7).

strong_actions: The seller sent a proposal and followed the customer's request to prepare a specified contract and commissioning scope (evidence 1, 2).
The seller collected filling-product details and asked about foaming before sending the information to technical staff (evidence 7).
weak_actions: A manager worklog reports repeated payment inquiries despite a stated payment date and a strongly negative customer reaction (evidence 5, 6).
manager_behavior.follow_up_quality: Follow-up continued across proposal, director review, contract, and technical clarification, but the payment contact cadence appears to have strained the relationship (evidence 3, 5, 6).
manager_behavior.next_step_control: The customer had supplied a payment date, but no receipt confirmation is shown; the filling-line requirements also needed a separate technical path (evidence 5, 7).

turning_points.description: The customer requested a specified contract and commissioning work after receiving the proposal (evidence 2).
The customer said the director had not yet returned a decision (evidence 3, 4).
The customer set a payment date, after which a worklog records frustration with repeated payment reminders (evidence 5, 6).
The call record introduces a separate filling-block specification (evidence 7).

primary_trajectory_explanation.category: director-gated purchase with payment follow-up friction
primary_trajectory_explanation.explanation: The labeling proposal advanced into contract and invoice processing, but decision authority sat with the director and payment timing remained unconfirmed. Repeated payment checking was reported as a source of customer friction; a second technical requirement appears late and may be separate (evidence 2, 3, 5, 6, 7).

secondary_factors: A filling-line requirement appears during payment follow-up, but its relation to the labeling purchase is unclear (evidence 7).
Payment timing is represented by a customer-stated date and a manager worklog, not a bank record (evidence 5, 6).

what_could_be_done: Agree one payment-check date and channel after the customer states a transfer date (evidence 5, 6).
Track the filling-line request separately until the customer confirms whether it is part of the same purchase (evidence 7).
limits: Director approval and the customer's finance process were outside the seller's direct control (evidence 3, 4).
The visible record ends before payment receipt or final technical scope is confirmed (evidence 5, 7).

uncertainties: The starting equipment brief is in a manager worklog and is not fully corroborated by direct customer language (evidence 0).
The reported negative response to payment reminders comes from a manager worklog, not a customer-authored statement (evidence 6).
The view does not confirm whether the stated payment date was met or whether the filling line was included in this deal (evidence 5, 7).

evidence.paraphrase: Manager log describes a PET-container labeling project, a target budget, and a planned August purchase.
Seller sends the requested labeling-equipment proposal and a video.
Customer sends packaging dimensions and asks the seller to prepare a contract with specification and commissioning work.
Customer says the director has not yet called back with a decision.
Customer again says the boss is not responding and no decision is available.
Customer says payment is planned for the following Tuesday.
Manager worklog says the customer reacted strongly to repeated payment questions and expected payment Thursday; this is a manager claim.
The call turns to a four-doser block for two canister types with different product viscosities, creating a possible additional project scope.
